title: Biologic Response to Crest to Restoration Distance in Subcrestally Placed Implants: A Case Report
content: Background: Subcrestally placed implants (SPI) offer biological and mechanical advantages, but their deeper positioning requires careful management of the peri-implant soft tissue interface, particularly the Crest to Restoration Distance (CRD). This vertical space, extending from the crestal bone to the implant restoration, plays a crucial role in maintaining peri-implant health. If CRD exceeds an optimal range, void formation can occur, increasing the risk of bacterial colonization, peri-implant mucositis, and eventual peri-implantitis. Optimizing CRD, including soft tissue thickness (STT), is essential for preserving peri-implant stability. Objective: This study aims to evaluate the influence of CRD optimization in peri-implant health by comparing two subcrestally placed implants in a split-mouth case. It further explores the structural role of peri-implant soft tissue, particularly the Transitional Zone (TZ) and Subcrestal Zone (SZ), in maintaining a stable biologic seal. Materials and Methods: Study Design: A split-mouth analysis involving two subcrestally placed implants (upper left and lower right first molars) in a 57-year-old female patient. 3D Analysis: Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) was utilized to measure CRD, Depth of Placement (DP), and Crest Restoration Length (CRL). Clinical Evaluation: Periodic assessments included Implant Paper Point Probing (IPPP), Bleeding on Probing (BOP), and other peri-implant health indicators. Intervention: A restoration adjustment was performed to optimize CRD at the test site (upper left implant). Results: Test Site (Upper Left Implant): Before optimization: Excessive CRD, deep probing depths (>3 mm), and clinical signs of mucositis (BOP, redness, swelling). After optimization: Adjusted CRD resolved mucositis symptoms, achieving stable probing depths (<1 mm), no BOP, and healthy peri-implant soft tissue. CBCT confirmed an improved biologic seal. Control Site (Lower Right Implant): Maintained a CRD within the optimal range from the beginning, with consistently healthy peri-implant tissues. No signs of peri-implant disease throughout the observation period. Conclusion: Maintaining an optimal CRD is associated with peri-implant soft tissue stability and may reduce the risk of sulcular epithelial downgrowth and pocket formation, potentially minimizing peri-implant disease. This study underscores the importance of considering 3D peri-implant soft tissue parameters in implant planning, particularly in subcrestally placed implants (SPI). Future research should focus on standardizing CRD guidelines to improve long-term implant outcomes.
